q: My plant keeps accounts April to March. Which reporting period do I use for CBAM embedded emissions data?
title: April to March accounts and CBAM periods
short: The calendar year, 1 January to 31 December. In the definitive period the Commission's guidance for operators and verifiers says an installation's CBAM reporting period is always the calendar year in which the goods were made. Keep fuel, power and production month by month, and read meters and count stock on both 1 January and 1 April.

ul: Your reporting period as an operator: the calendar year of production. Guidance No. 1 ties this to the definition of reporting period in the Methodology Act.
Verification of a year cannot finish before January of the next year, because the verifier needs data up to 31 December.

Your importer's CBAM declaration covers goods imported in the previous calendar year and is due by 30 September. For 2026 imports, that is 30 September 2027, and the guidance suggests importers want verified reports by mid-August.
No reporting period before 2026 is accepted.

sections.h: One line in the Q&A says otherwise
p: The Commission's CBAM Questions and Answers, updated 15 October 2026, still says a different reference period such as a financial year may be used if it covers at least three consecutive months, is representative and is applied consistently. The definitive-period guidance documents for operators and for verifiers both say calendar year, always. Plan on the calendar year. If you want to rely on the Q&A line, get your verifier's agreement in writing before you collect a year of data that way.

sections.h: Two periods, one set of meter readings
p: The verification guidance uses exactly this case as its example: CBAM runs January to December while another system runs April to March. A gas meter read only on 1 April, or a coal pile counted only at the March close, leaves a hole in the CBAM year. Read the meters and take stock on both 1 January and 1 April, and monthly if you can, so no month has to be guessed.

Counting coal, precursors and finished goods at midnight on 31 December is rarely practical. Verifiers may accept a cut-off up to one or two working days away, for example 30 December at 18:00, if you fix the time in advance, measure emissions, production and stocks as close to it as you can, document it, and start the next year from the same point.

sections.h: Steps for a plant on April to March books
ol: Split every fuel invoice and electricity bill into the month it relates to, not the month it was paid.
Record production in tonnes for each month for each CBAM product, counting only goods that meet sale specifications.
For a calendar year, take January to March from one fiscal year and April to December from the next.
Work out specific embedded emissions: total attributed emissions divided by tonnes produced in the same months.
Write the period, the cut-off and the method in your monitoring plan, and keep the monthly workings for the verifier.

p: An electricity bill for 15 December to 14 January covers two calendar years. Split it by meter readings if you have them, otherwise by days. Use one method consistently and record it.

example.title: Worked example: building calendar 2026 from two fiscal years
lines: January to March 2026 (from FY 2025-26): 3,150 t CO2 and 5,000 t of product
April to December 2026 (from FY 2026-27): 9,450 t CO2 and 15,000 t of product
Specific embedded emissions: 12,600 / 20,000 = 0.63 t CO2 per tonne

senseible: Senseible stores each record against its billing period, so emissions can be totalled for any 12-month window, calendar or fiscal, and its CBAM Suite builds the calendar-year operator report by production process. You still enter production tonnes from your own books.
